overview:
Shortly after dawn on 7 October 2023, several thousand fighters led by Hamas broke through the fence around the Gaza Strip under a barrage of rockets and attacked Israeli army posts, farming communities and an open-air music festival in the western Negev. About 1,200 people were killed, most of them civilians, and 251 were taken back into Gaza as hostages — the deadliest single day in Israel's history and the deadliest for Jews since the Holocaust. Israel declared war, imposed a near-total siege on the territory's roughly 2.2 million residents, and began an air campaign of extraordinary intensity, followed on 27 October by a ground invasion. Over the next two years the fighting moved south through Gaza City, Khan Yunis and finally Rafah on the Egyptian border, driving almost the entire population from their homes, often repeatedly, into a shrinking strip of coastal encampments. Individual episodes became international flashpoints in their own right: the explosion at al-Ahli Arab Hospital in October 2023, whose cause was disputed within hours; the repeated strikes on Jabalia refugee camp; the killing of five-year-old Hind Rajab and the paramedics sent to reach her; the crowd killed around an aid convoy in Gaza City in February 2024 that Palestinians call the Flour Massacre.

The war never stayed inside Gaza. Hezbollah opened a front from Lebanon within days, emptying border villages on both sides before Israel escalated in September 2024 with the pager attacks and the strike that killed Hassan Nasrallah at Hezbollah's headquarters in Beirut. The Houthis in Yemen fired at Israel and at shipping in the Red Sea, disrupting a significant share of world trade. Israel and Iran traded direct missile fire for the first time, and Israeli operations reached Damascus, Tehran and, in September 2025, Doha — a strike on Hamas negotiators in the capital of the Gulf state that was mediating the talks. Ismail Haniyeh, the movement's political leader, was assassinated in Tehran in July 2024; Yahya Sinwar, the architect of 7 October, was killed in Gaza that October. Inside Gaza the humanitarian collapse deepened until, in August 2025, the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification confirmed famine in Gaza Governorate — the first ever declared in the Middle East — with more than half a million people in catastrophic conditions.

Three ceasefires punctuated the war: a week-long pause in November 2023 that returned some hostages, a longer truce from January 2025 that broke down in March, and the agreement of 10 October 2025 under a United States–brokered plan, which brought back the remaining living hostages and an Israeli pullback to agreed lines. Implementation has proceeded unevenly since, with Hamas standing down its civil administration while questions of disarmament, Israeli withdrawal and reconstruction remain unsettled. The legal reckoning runs in parallel. South Africa filed a genocide case against Israel at the International Court of Justice on 29 December 2023; the Court ordered provisional measures in January, March and May 2024, and the merits are still being briefed. In November 2024 the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants for Benjamin Netanyahu and Yoav Gallant, alongside one for a senior Hamas commander, and a United Nations commission of inquiry later concluded that acts of genocide had been committed. Israel rejects those findings.
significance: More than any conflict since 2003, this war reorganised the politics of the Middle East and strained the institutions built after 1945 to constrain war. It shattered the assumption, held in Israel and abroad, that Gaza could be indefinitely contained and the Palestinian question indefinitely deferred; it drew Iran and Israel into open, direct exchanges of fire for the first time and hollowed out Hezbollah's deterrent posture; and it interrupted the Gulf–Israel normalisation that had seemed the region's dominant trend in 2023. It also produced the first famine ever formally confirmed in the region, a scale of urban destruction with few modern parallels, and a set of proceedings at the ICJ and ICC that will test for years whether international humanitarian law can bind states with powerful protectors. Its effects on Western domestic politics, on the credibility of the United Nations system, and on a generation of Palestinians and Israelis raised inside it will outlast the ceasefire by a long way.
coverage: Written from the Wikipedia and Britannica overviews, the ICJ's own case file, the WHO announcement of the August 2025 IPC famine confirmation, and OCHA's casualty methodology page; the dataset's own 52 events skew heavily toward discrete attacks and killings in 2023–2025, which is why this story's stated span of 2023 ends well before the fighting did, and one entry is dated 2020 in error. Casualty totals are the biggest genuine unknown: Gaza's health ministry figures, above 70,000 dead and rising, are the only systematic count and are contested by Israel, while OCHA has declined to enter any of them into its verified database and epidemiological work in The Lancet argues the true toll including indirect deaths is considerably higher. Reporting from inside Gaza has been shaped throughout by Israel's exclusion of foreign journalists and by the deaths of well over a hundred Palestinian reporters, so contemporaneous accounts of individual incidents — the al-Ahli hospital explosion above all — often rest on partisan claims that remain unresolved.
